reason: Cell junctions appear to connect neighboring surface cells, helping form a protective layer.

reason: The skin support cells and connective fibers appear to belong together in the skin's supporting tissue.
expectation: They will form a supportive skin layer.

effect: The support cells and fibers formed a supporting skin layer with capillaries, ready to join the surface layer.
reaction: The tug illustration helps show how the fibers provide support.
reason: The connected surface sheet and supporting layer appear to be complementary parts of the skin.
expectation: The layers will join to form a skin structure.

reaction: The automatic combination clarified the required order, and the distinction between dead outer cells and living layers was useful.
reason: The completed surface barrier and supporting skin layer appear to be complementary parts of the skin.
expectation: The barrier and support will join into a layered skin structure.

effect: The barrier and supporting layer formed layered skin, with nutrients and oxygen reaching the living surface cells from vessels below.
reaction: The cross-section makes the connection between circulation and the surface cells clear.
reason: Skin sensory endings should add the contact sensing needed for the current goal.

reason: The arm needs the sensitive skin for protection and touch.
expectation: The skin will cover the arm and add contact sensing.

effect: The sensitive skin now covers the arm and connects to its nerves; the open vessels show where the body supply network belongs.
reaction: The open vessel ends make the next connection clear.
reason: The body supply network can connect to the arm's vessels and provide continuing supplies.

effect: The arm is now connected to the body supply network, and the remaining goal is to hold the glass steady using contact feedback.
reaction: The upper-body cutaway brings the previously built systems together.
reason: The living body model has the sensing and control needed to interact with the glass.
expectation: The hand will use contact feedback to hold the glass steady.

effect: The final combination completed the goal and showed how touch signals and muscle action help steady a slipping glass.
reaction: The slipping-and-correction sequence made the purpose of contact feedback clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Holding the glass was most worthwhile because the sequence connected touch, nerves and muscle action to a familiar task.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the surface and supporting layers was briefly confusing because the surface needed its outer layer first, although the compatibility feedback resolved it.

surprise.text: I found it useful to learn that the outermost skin cells are dead while living layers beneath replace them.

arbitrary.text: The required order for adding the tough outer layer was not clear to me before the compatibility feedback, though its protective purpose became clear afterward.

continue.text: I would probably continue for another chapter: seeing the assembled systems work together to steady the glass was interesting, though several layer-building steps felt predictable.
